So the bounds are subexponential as $n\to\infty$, but the proof certifies no speed-up over brute force for any input of bounded density that could ever be written down. Third, for the clause-product form of the interpolation algorithm we prove limits in a cost model matching the preprint's evaluation. By a short algebraic lemma, polynomial cost needs components of $O(\log^3 n)$ variables with per-point evaluation, or primal treewidth $O(\log^2 n)$ with dynamic programming over the groups. So the scheme costs $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\mathrm{tw}})}$ at treewidth $\mathrm{tw}$, $2^{\Omega(\sqrt n)}$ with high probability on random 3-CNF above clause density 3, and $2^{\Omega(n^{1/3})}$ even on trivially countable path formulas. We explain why the preprint's sharper routes escape these limits. Fourth, we report experiments.
item.dc:creator: Fabio Dias, Yvens Lima

item.title: Compressed Oracle Duality: A simple framework for knowing what quantum adversaries know
item.description: arXiv:2611.00609v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given a quantum adversary that queries a random oracle, how do we characterize the information that they "know"? The Compressed Oracle method of Zhandry (CRYPTO 2019) is one method that records the queries that the adversary makes; this recording serves as a representation of the information that is learned. However, a significant limitation of the Compressed Oracle method is that it may continue to store information that the adversary has "forgotten." This issue is especially pertinent in the space-bounded setting, where the adversary may uncompute information to free up space, while the information may still reside in the compressed oracle. In this work, we present a simple and interpretable framework called "Compressed Oracle Duality," which extends the Compressed Oracle method for space-bounded algorithms. By applying an isometry to the memory of a quantum adversary, we obtain a pair of compressed oracles with identical marginal distributions and classical correlations which correspond to the knowledge the adversary retains. In fact, we show that the outcome of measuring the new compressed oracle database corresponds exactly to applying the pretty-good measurement on the adversary's memory. As an application of our framework for collision search, we give a simplified proof of the recent $T^2S = \Omega(N\log N)$ quantum time-space tradeoff for label-symmetric algorithms due to Magniez-Zur (arXiv:2609.10808); we also prove a stronger classical tradeoff of $TS=\Omega(N\log N)$ assuming label symmetry. The proofs under our framework do not require representation theory and instead bound the mutual information between the compressed oracle pairs. This highlights both how the label symmetry assumption bypasses known proof barriers as well as the challenges that remain in achieving unconditional quantum time-space tradeoffs.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Ding, Mark Zhandry

item.title: Differential Privacy for Generalized Entropy Indices of Income Inequality
item.description: arXiv:2611.00888v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The mean log deviation and the Theil index are two widely used measures of income inequality. The organization releasing these measures may be obligated to protect the confidentiality of the individual incomes used in the computations. In particular, the organization may wish to release versions of these measures with formal guarantees of privacy. The organization could do so by satisfying differential privacy; however, typical applications of differentially private algorithms are likely to add so much noise to the measures that they become unusable. We present differentially private algorithms for these indices with reasonable error properties. The algorithms rely on computing or approximating bounds on the smooth sensitivity, that is, the maximum absolute amount the inequality measures change when replacing any subset of the $n$ incomes in the reported data with arbitrarily chosen feasible values. For the mean log deviation, the algorithm runs in $O(n^2)$ time. For the Theil index, the algorithm runs in $O(n\log n)$ time. We illustrate the performance of each differentially private algorithm using individual-level and household-level income data from the Current Population Survey. We also examine repeated sampling properties of the algorithms using artificially generated data. The empirical results indicate when these differentially private algorithms can be expected to provide accurate estimates and when they are likely to introduce too much noise.
item.dc:creator: Jiahe Li, Jerome P. Reiter

item.title: Shared Randomness and Parallel Rounds in Permutation Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2611.01028v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the shared randomness needed to sample a uniform permutation in parallel output rounds. Coordinates committed in the same round are independent conditional on the complete history and the current shared choice. Previous outputs are public; local computation and private randomness are free. We charge each shared choice by the logarithm of its conditional support size and sum these costs along the worst execution path. At every fixed round density $\rho\in(0,1)$, the optimal limiting total-variation error under any $o(n)$ shared budget matches the conditional-marginal optimum, even with arbitrary local kernels and adaptive coordination. A fixed improvement requires linear cost. For exact sampling in $R=\Theta(n)$ rounds, the optimum is $n\Phi(R/n)+O(\log n)$, where $\Phi$ linearly interpolates $\Phi(1/q)=\log q$. A protocol attaining this rate uses an initial seed and at most one further binary shared choice. When $\lceil n/2\rceil\le R\le n$, the finite optimum is $\log\binom{2(n-R)}{n-R}$, attained by an initial seed alone. The approximate converse uses an entropy inequality for sparse injections to control overlap with the target. The exact construction reuses randomness retained in a shared label partition after the first-stage outputs are exposed.
item.dc:creator: Haoxiang Huang

item.title: How Much Can Approximate Equilibria Change the Social Cost of Selfish Routing?
item.description: arXiv:2611.01234v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study approximate Nash equilibria in nonatomic congestion games, with the goal of understanding how much the social cost can change when the equilibrium condition is relaxed. We consider $\epsilon$-approximate Nash equilibria ($\epsilon$-NE), in which each player uses a strategy whose cost is at most $1 + \epsilon$ times the minimum available cost. We compare the social costs of $\epsilon$-NE and exact Nash equilibria. This lets us quantify, for example, how much a navigation app can reduce total travel time when drivers tolerate routes slightly slower than the fastest available route. For degree-$d$ polynomial latencies in both general nonatomic congestion games and single-commodity routing games on series-parallel networks, we give tight lower and upper bounds on the relative change in social cost from an exact Nash equilibrium to any $\epsilon$-NE, with matching instances for every $\epsilon$. For small $\epsilon$, the largest possible relative reduction and increase in general congestion games are both $\Theta(\sqrt{d\epsilon})$, independently of the number of resources and populations. In contrast, on series-parallel networks of depth $h$, the largest possible relative reduction is $\Theta(h\epsilon)$, while the largest possible relative increase is known to be $\epsilon$. For the classes of games we study, these results give a tight and quantitative characterization of the possible changes in social cost and establish a separation between general and series-parallel networks.
item.dc:creator: Yu Cheng, Tianle Jiang

item.title: A Numerical Refinement of an Exact Discrete Fourier Transform Bound
item.description: arXiv:2611.01257v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We refine the numerical bounds in Kartal's instantiation of Sussman's exact discrete Fourier transform construction. For every integer n >= 1, the resulting algorithm computes the length-n transform with work O(n (log n)^(1 - delta)), where delta = 0.0030201659. The bound holds in an exact complex-arithmetic RAM model with a supplied canonical root of unity. This final exponent saving exceeds the earlier certified parameter C_0 = 0.00302016 by 5.9 x 10^(-9). We retain the underlying circuit, tighten rational bounds for sums of powers of its block and target ranks, and increase the fixed tensor power from 7760 to 11640. These bounds establish the inequalities for Sussman's recursion at the intermediate certificate parameter C = 0.00302016595. The gap C - delta absorbs the overhead of recursion and Fourier reduction. The resulting transform theorem is proved in Lean and checked against the reference problem statement.
item.dc:creator: Zhihao Yao, Sichao Liu

item.title: A Decomposition Theorem and a Simple Algorithm for Contraction Fixed Points
item.description: arXiv:2611.01302v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove a decomposition theorem for the problem of computing an approximate fixed point of a contraction map $f\colon [0,1]^k \to [0,1]^k$ under the $\ell_{\infty}$-norm. After a preliminary version of the decomposition theorem appeared on arXiv [CLY26], Feodorov and Haslebacher [FH26] gave a striking application of the theorem, showing that it can be used to convert any $\operatorname{poly}(k,\log(1/\varepsilon))$-query algorithm with running time $(k\log(1/\varepsilon))^{O(k)}$ into an algorithm with running time $(k\log(1/\varepsilon))^{O(\sqrt{k})}$. They instantiated this framework with an $O(k^2\log(1/\varepsilon))$-query algorithm with the desired running time, thereby obtaining the first subexponential-time algorithm for contraction fixed points under the $\ell_{\infty}$-norm and, via well-known reductions, the first deterministic subexponential-time algorithm for simple stochastic games and mean-payoff games. In addition to the decomposition theorem, as our second main result in this paper, we show that the $O(k\log(1/\varepsilon))$-query algorithm of [CLY25] can be implemented in time $(k\log(1/\varepsilon))^{O(k)}$; our algorithm may be viewed as conceptually simpler compared to the algorithm of [FH26]. A key observation here is that the function constructed in [CLY25], whose fixed points are used as the next query points, turns out to be nonexpansive under the $\ell_{\infty}$-norm, so the brute-force procedure can be replaced by known algorithms for contraction fixed points.
item.dc:creator: Xi Chen, Yuhao Li, Mihalis Yannakakis

item.title: Metric Testing: A Characterization of One-Sided Testability
item.description: arXiv:2611.01346v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give a unified framework for one-sided testability (constant-query testing) of metric families. For a broad class of families defined by fixed local predicates, we prove that testability is equivalent to two structural properties: \emph{packing amplification}, which turns many edge-disjoint local violations into a positive density of violations, and \emph{completion stability}, which allows locally consistent partial matrices with few missing entries to be cheaply completed. This characterization yields a common proof strategy and simpler proofs of classical testability results for ultrametrics, tree pseudometrics, Euclidean pseudometrics in fixed dimension, and several others. Our framework also gives new quantitative bounds for metric testing: a nonadaptive one-sided upper bound for matrices with entries in the bounded range $[1,C]$, and two-sided nonadaptive and adaptive lower bounds for general metrics.
item.dc:creator: Zihan Tan, Theo Teske

item.title: Three-phase time minimization transportation problem with non-idle phases: a polynomial two-witness algorithm
item.description: arXiv:2611.01387v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The three-phase time minimization transportation problem partitions the origin-terminal links into three sets used in consecutive phases and minimizes the sum of the phase shipment times. Optimal solutions may leave a phase idle, as in the main example of the original study. We require every phase to carry a positive integer quantity while leaving the split of the total requirement across phases free. Discarding idle solutions from the original algorithm does not, in general, solve this variant. We prove that the optimum is attained by fixing one witness link in each of two phases and deciding the third phase by a single network flow computation, with the optimal Phase-3 time of each witness pair located by binary search. The resulting exact algorithm is strongly polynomial. It extends to any fixed number of phases, whereas, when the number of phases is part of the input, even non-idle feasibility is strongly NP-complete; feasibility alone is fixed-parameter tractable in the number of phases via known rainbow-matching results. We also characterize the minimum time of each phase. On the main example, non-idleness raises the optimum from 38 to 41. On 3,650 random instances with up to $50\times50$ links the algorithm took at most 50.2 seconds, and non-idleness raised the optimal value in 41% of the 2,250 instances with equal phase sizes; on 90 sampled instances it was faster than a mixed integer programming solver on 80 with a direct formulation and on 65 with a tighter threshold formulation.
item.dc:creator: Sailesh Kamalahasan, Raghav Paladugu, Archana Khurana

item.title: Smoothed analysis of stability radii for the assignment problem
item.description: arXiv:2611.01584v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Every linear program can tolerate small changes to its costs and still yield a solution of the original problem. The size of this tolerance measures how robust an optimal decision is to noise or numerical error, and how much regularization the problem can support. Classical sensitivity analysis can determine this tolerance only from an optimal solution. This paper provides a priori lower bounds on two measures of this tolerance -- the optimality gap and the $\infty$-norm stability radius -- for the $n$-by-$n$ linear assignment problem over the Birkhoff polytope. The bounds derive from a smoothed analysis, which adds Gaussian noise with standard deviation of at least $\sigma$ in every direction to an arbitrary base cost. At every fixed confidence level, uniformly over the base cost, both quantities are at least of order $\sigma/(n\sqrt{\log n})$. The radius bound is asymptotically sharp. Under isotropic noise, the worst case occurs when every assignment has equal cost, and in this case, a scaled stability radius converges in distribution to a standard exponential variable.
item.dc:creator: Michael P. Friedlander

item.title: Fine-Grained Complexity Across the Computational Phase Transition
item.description: arXiv:2611.02702v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How does a computational problem transition from easy to hard? In the hard-core model, approximate counting and sampling are polynomial-time tractable up to tree uniqueness, but worst-case intractable at any constant relative distance above it unless $\mathsf{NP}=\mathsf{RP}$. We quantify the transition from polynomial to exponential mixing for classical Glauber dynamics. On $n$-vertex graphs of maximum degree $d\ge3$, at fugacity $\lambda=(1+\delta)\lambda_{\mathrm c}(d)$ with sufficiently small $\delta\ge0$ that may vanish with $n$, its worst-case mixing time has the form $\exp\{\Theta(n\delta^2/d)\}n^{1+\Theta(1)}$. The upper bound is degree-uniform, and the matching lower bound holds for every fixed $d$. Annealing gives approximate counting with the same running-time upper bound at fixed accuracy. For general sampling and counting algorithms, we establish a robust fine-grained reduction from SAT without assuming a lower bound on SAT's running time. For any fixed $d\ge3$ and $0<\gamma<1$, a sampling or approximate-counting algorithm running in $\exp\{O((n\delta^2/d)^{1-\gamma})\}\operatorname{poly}(n)$ time along any one suitable inverse-polynomial distance sequence $\delta=\delta(n)$, yields a randomized SAT algorithm running in $\exp\{\widetilde O(s^{1-\gamma})\}$ time on inputs of binary length $s$. This power-saving transfer identifies $n\delta^2/d$ as the analogue of SAT input length for hard-core sampling and counting at relative distance $\delta$ above criticality: beating the Glauber exponent by a fixed power through any sampling or counting method would yield a corresponding power improvement for SAT. At criticality, we establish $O(\sqrt{n/d})$ spectral independence, optimal in $n$ at fixed degree, and degree-uniform Glauber mixing in $\widetilde O(n(n/d)^{1+1/(d-2)})$ time, improving the previous $\widetilde O(n^{4+4/(d-2)})$ bound.
item.dc:creator: Zhe Ju, Jingcheng Liu, Yitong Yin

item.title: Full-Rank Constructions of Explicit Lossless Expanders and Good Small-Set qLTCs
item.description: arXiv:2611.02963v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We construct explicit two-sided lossless expanders whose binary adjacency matrices have full rank, and use them to obtain explicit asymptotically good quantum LDPC codes whose specified X- and Z-check matrices have full row rank and satisfy small-set soundness, or confinement, on a linear range. Our lossless expanders are a variant of those of Hsieh, Lubotzky, Mohanty, Reiner, and Zhang, with a free action of a finite 2-group. Under such an action, injectivity and surjectivity of the adjacency matrix are detected on a fixed-size matrix indexed by vertex orbits. Adding a sparse factor to the gadget at the middle vertices of a single type then enforces full rank, with a controlled loss in expansion. To obtain the 2-group action, we observe that reducing the generators of the Lubotzky-Phillips-Sarnak Ramanujan graphs modulo powers of 2, instead of modulo an odd prime, gives Ramanujan Cayley graphs on finite 2-groups. This construction may be of independent interest. Plugging two such expanders into the balanced product of Lin and Hsieh gives the quantum codes, since full rank of the input graphs is inherited by the check matrices. Our construction supplies the code family sought by Hong, Guo, and Lucas. Applying their analysis, within their framework and under their dynamical assumptions, gives quantum memories whose free-energy density is analytic at every positive temperature and whose guaranteed lifetime is $exp(\Omega(N))$ at sufficiently low fixed positive temperature, where N is the blocklength. This improves the previously guaranteed stretched-exponential timescale.
item.dc:creator: Yali Aharon-Holzman, Michael Ilan, Assaf Reiner, Amnon Ta-Shma

item.title: Asymptotically Optimal Weighted Edge Colorings via Local Bin Packing
item.description: arXiv:2611.03190v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study weighted edge coloring, where each edge of a graph $G$ has a weight in $(0,1]$, and colors are assigned so that the incident weight of each color at every vertex is at most one. The objective is to minimize the number of colors, denoted by $\chi'_w(G)$. This generalizes classical edge coloring (all weights are one) and bin packing ($G$ is a star). Two natural lower bounds are the maximum weighted degree $\Delta_w(G)$ and the maximum local bin-packing number $\mathrm{bp}(G)$: the maximum, over vertices, of the minimum number of unit bins needed to pack the incident weights. We have $\lceil\Delta_w(G)\rceil\le\mathrm{bp}(G)\le\chi'_w(G)$. How closely these local lower bounds approximate the global optimum is a longstanding open problem. Our main result establishes an asymptotic weighted analogue of Vizing's theorem: every simple graph admits a coloring using at most $(1+o(1))\mathrm{bp}(G)$ colors. Thus local bin packings can be made globally consistent with asymptotically vanishing relative loss, even in nonbipartite graphs. Our local-to-global rounding framework coordinates feasible local packing distributions into a partial coloring, leaving only $o(\mathrm{bp}(G))$ uncolored weight at every vertex. For bipartite multigraphs, we prove $\chi'_w(G)\le(2+o(1))\Delta_w(G)$, establishing the Chung--Ross conjecture [SICOMP'91] asymptotically. For loopless multigraphs, we obtain the exact bound $\chi'_w(G)\le3\lceil\Delta_w(G)\rceil$. Both leading coefficients are optimal, giving weighted analogues of the classical K\H{o}nig--Shannon bounds. Further upper and lower bounds show that the classical factor-$3/2$ separation does not persist with the local bin-packing benchmark. We also disprove the exact weighted-degree conjecture of Feige and Singh [ESA'08]. Our upper bounds have polynomial-time algorithms, and their existence statements are formalized in Lean 4.
item.dc:creator: Rishikesh Gajjala, Arindam Khan

item.title: Calibrated Multiaccuracy: Deterministic and Randomized Sample Complexity
item.description: arXiv:2611.03305v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Calibrated multiaccuracy asks that a predictor be globally calibrated and multiaccurate with respect to a bounded test family $G$; that is, its residuals should be uncorrelated with every test $g(x)\in G$. This weakening of multicalibration suffices for many applications. Its sample complexity was not known to improve on that of full multicalibration, which is $\widetilde\Theta\left(\frac{\log|G|}{\varepsilon^2} + \frac{1}{\varepsilon^{3}}\right)$ when $|G|$ is at least a sufficiently large power of $\log(1/\varepsilon)$. We resolve the sample complexity of $\varepsilon$-calibrated multiaccuracy, showing that it scales as $$ \widetilde\Theta\left(\frac{\log|G|}{\varepsilon^2} + \frac{1}{\varepsilon^{5/2}}\right), $$ separating it from the complexity of multicalibration. The upper bound is obtained by an algorithm that outputs a randomized predictor. For deterministic predictors, we establish the tight rate $$ \widetilde\Theta\left( \frac{\log|G|}{\varepsilon^2} + \frac{(\log|G|)^{1/3}}{\varepsilon^{8/3}} \right) $$ whenever $\log|G|=\Omega(\log(1/\varepsilon))$. When $\log|G|\le\varepsilon^{-1+\kappa}$ for any fixed $\kappa\in(0,1)$, this rate is polynomially larger than the rate for randomized predictors. Thus, unlike for multicalibration, calibrated multiaccuracy exhibits a genuine sample-complexity separation between deterministic and randomized predictors. The matching upper and lower bounds show that the unusual cube-root dependence on $\log|G|$ is intrinsic. At $\log|G|\asymp\varepsilon^{-1}$, the minimax rates for randomized and deterministic calibrated multiaccuracy both coincide with the minimax rate for multicalibration.
item.dc:creator: Jiuyao Lu, Georgy Noarov, Aaron Roth

item.title: Online Algorithms Cannot Find Isolated Perceptron Solutions
item.description: arXiv:2611.03397v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The binary perceptron problem asks for a length-$n$ sign vector in the intersection of $\lfloor \alpha n\rfloor$-many independent random Gaussian half-spaces. A striking feature of this model is strong freezing: at every constraint density $\alpha > 0$, all but a vanishing fraction of solutions are isolated -- $\Omega(n)$-far from all others, in Hamming distance. Such solutions are believed to be algorithmically inaccessible. Nevertheless, efficient algorithms find solutions at some constraint densities $\alpha$. One possible resolution of this apparent contradiction is that the solution space also contains rare well-connected structures, and that algorithms succeed by locating them. Gong, Huang, Li and Sellke (FOCS 2026) proved this for stable algorithms, by showing that such algorithms cannot locate isolated solutions with probability more than $\approx 0.84$. In this work, we study online algorithms, which receive the columns of the constraint matrix one by one and sign each irrevocably upon arrival. This is a widely used class of algorithms in discrepancy minimization, and it includes the algorithm of Jo and Lee (2026), which has one of the best provable guarantees for the binary perceptron. We prove that at any constraint density, any online algorithm outputs an isolated solution with probability $o(1)$. Our proof is based on the observation that the signs an online algorithm has already fixed can be completed to at most one isolated solution, so a successful algorithm must choose the unique correct sign for each of the last few columns. Using the exchangeability of these columns, we show that such an algorithm must match a suffix-parallel baseline, which signs each of them as if it were the next column to arrive. We then use an anti-concentration argument to show that such a baseline rarely produces a unique completion.
item.dc:creator: Shuangping Li, Gabe Schoenbach

item.title: Should We Combine Our Data? Algorithms and Limits for Privately Assessing Data Sharing
item.description: arXiv:2611.03599v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we study when two parties should pool their data to train a machine learning model. Two agents, Alice and Bob, each hold a sensitive labeled dataset and want to train a classifier from a given hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$. Even when each party's dataset can be perfectly classified on its own, the two parties may follow conflicting labeling standards or have selection biases that affect their features and label sets, such that no single classifier in $\mathcal{H}$ fits their combined data. Before committing to data sharing, Alice and Bob therefore want to test whether a single classifier in $\mathcal{H}$ can jointly fit both datasets---without revealing their individual data points to one another. We formalize this problem from a learning-theoretic viewpoint via $\operatorname{opt}_\mathcal{H}$, the minimum \emph{number of mistakes} made by any hypothesis in $\mathcal{H}$ on their pooled data. Through interactive communication, the agents must distinguish $\operatorname{opt}_\mathcal{H}=0$ (compatible datasets) from $\operatorname{opt}_\mathcal{H}\geq t$ (conflicting datasets) under pure $\varepsilon$-two-party differential privacy. A trusted curator could do this with $t=O(1/\varepsilon)$, and we ask how small $t$ can be without one. For thresholds on the real line over a domain of size $m$, we show that the optimal $t$ is $\tilde{\Theta}(\log\log m/\varepsilon)$, exponentially smaller than the $\Theta(\log m/\varepsilon)$ samples needed to privately learn thresholds, even with a curator. For halfspaces in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the dependence on $m$ jumps to $\log(m)$: we give a protocol with $t=\tilde{O}(d^3\log m/\varepsilon)$ and show that some domains require $t=\Omega(d\log(m/d)/\varepsilon)$.
item.dc:creator: Mahdi Haghifam, Kumar Kshitij Patel, Avrim Blum, Giulia Fanti, Juba Ziani

item.title: A Simple Randomized Estimator for Harmonic Numbers and Logarithms
item.description: arXiv:1704.04538v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scanning a list of $x$ distinct numbers in uniformly random order for its maximum replaces the running maximum $H_x$ times on average, where $H_x$ is the $x$th harmonic number. Run backwards, this gives an estimator: the replacement count of a random list is an unbiased Monte Carlo estimate of $H_x$, and since $H_x = \ln x + \gamma + O(1/x)$, a corrected estimate of $\ln x$. We give the exact variance of the count, an error decomposition with sample-size rules, and an exact sampler of the count using $H_x$ integer draws on average instead of a scan of length $x$. Coupling two counts estimates $\ln(a/b)$ without $\gamma$, and a binary range reduction then bounds the standard error by $\sqrt{\ln 2/n}$ for every $x$ at fewer than $1.7$ draws per repetition on average. A classical deterministic series on the same reduction reaches the rounding floor with sixteen terms in the reported experiments, quantifying the gap between the two approaches. The purpose is pedagogical: the analysis of an algorithm becomes an estimator of the quantity that analysis produces, with exact variances, finite-sample error bounds, reproducible experiments, and machine-checked algorithm contracts and moment identities. The ingredients are classical; the contribution is their assembly.
item.dc:creator: Ali Dasdan

item.title: Tight (Double) Exponential Bounds for Identification Problems: Locating-Dominating Set and Test Cover
item.description: arXiv:2402.08346v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate fine-grained algorithmic aspects for classical identification problems in graphs, namely LOCATING-DOMINATING SET, and in set systems, namely TEST COVER. In the first problem, an input is a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices and an integer $k$, and the objective is to decide whether there is a subset $S$ of $k$ vertices such that any two distinct vertices not in $S$ are dominated by distinct subsets of $S$. In the second problem, an input is a set $U$ of items, a collection $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of $U$ called tests, and an integer $k$, and the objective is to select a set $S$ of at most $k$ tests such that any two distinct items are contained in a distinct subset of tests of $S$. For our first result, we show that LOCATING-DOMINATING SET (respectively, TEST COVER) parameterized by the treewidth of the input graph (respectively, the incidence graph) does not admit an algorithm running in time $2^{2^{o(\textsf{tw})}} \cdot {\rm poly}(n)$ (respectively, $2^{2^{o(\textsf{tw})}} \cdot {\rm poly}(|U| + |\mathcal{F}|)$), unless the ETH fails. Next, we prove that, unless the ETH fails, LOCATING-DOMINATING SET does not admit an algorithm running in time $2^{o(k^2)} \cdot {\rm poly}(n)$, nor a polynomial-time kernelization algorithm that reduces the solution size and outputs a kernel with $2^{o(k)}$ vertices, and TEST COVER does not admit an algorithm running in time $2^{2^{o(k)}} \cdot {\rm poly}(|U| + |\mathcal{F}|)$ nor a kernel with $2^{2^{o(k)}}$ vertices. Again, we show that these lower bounds are tight by designing (kernelization) algorithms with matching running times.
