item.title: Theoretical Analysis of Byte-Pair Encoding
item.description: arXiv:2411.08671v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) is a widely used method for subword tokenization, with origins in grammar-based text compression. It is employed in a variety of language processing tasks such as machine translation or large language model (LLM) pretraining, to create a token dictionary of a prescribed size. Most evaluations of BPE to date are empirical, and the reasons for its good practical performance are not well understood. In this paper we focus on the optimization problem underlying BPE: finding a pair encoding that achieves optimal compression utility. We show that this problem is APX-complete, indicating that it is unlikely to admit a polynomial-time approximation scheme. This answers, in a stronger form, a question recently raised by Zouhar et al. On the positive side, we show that BPE approximates the compression utility of the optimal pair encoding to a worst-case factor between $1/3$ and $(1-e^{-2})/2 \approx 0.4324$. Our results aim to explain the ongoing success of BPE and are, to our knowledge, the first rigorous guarantees on its compression utility that hold for all inputs.
item.dc:creator: L\'aszl\'o Kozma, Johannes Voderholzer

item.title: Gain-Sharing Optimization in Randomized Primal--Dual Analysis: Structure and Certification
item.description: arXiv:2503.09508v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Randomized primal--dual guarantees for online matching and allocation often depend on a gain-sharing function that determines how algorithmic gains are distributed among dual variables and, in some settings, also affects allocation decisions. We study the best certificate obtainable by optimizing this function within a specified algorithm--analysis template. For an admissible function class F, we formulate the problem as the functional optimization $\Gamma(F)=\sup_{f\in F} L[f]$, where $L[f]$ is the worst-case expected dual-feasibility factor. We develop two complementary certification methods: auxiliary linear programs with explicit finite-grid error bounds, and a continuous approach based on monotone Volterra comparison and residual-based numerical verification. We apply them to the vertex-weighted Stochastic Balance template for online matching with stochastic rewards under uniform vanishing success probabilities. For the configuration-LP benchmark and specified dual updates, we optimize over the full admissible class $F_0$ of continuous non-decreasing functions from $[0,\infty)$ to $[0,1]$, and prove $\Gamma(F_0)\in[0.5802,0.5805]$. We also show that the more tractable subclass used for auxiliary-LP certification attains the same optimum.
item.dc:creator: Pan Xu

item.title: An Efficient Frequency-Based Approach for Maximal Square Detection in Binary Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2503.18974v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present FreqBased, a frequency-based algorithm for the maximal square problem in binary matrices. The algorithm maintains a vertical run-length array and a horizontal counter to validate candidate squares, matching the standard single-array dynamic programming algorithm in O(mn) time and O(n) space while reducing the amount of work performed during execution. Experiments on synthetic random binary matrices reveal a clear density-dependent performance transition: FreqBased consistently outperforms the dynamic programming baseline on moderate- and high-density inputs across Intel and AMD processors, achieving peak speedups of 1.175x and 1.277x, respectively, while executing up to 2.08x fewer instructions. On 180 real aerial image masks from the INRIA dataset, FreqBased outperforms the baseline on every instance with speedups of up to 4.63x, confirming that the instruction-count advantage observed on synthetic inputs extends to real binary matrices with spatial structure. Hardware performance counter analysis shows that the performance advantage arises primarily from reduced instruction count despite lower execution efficiency, demonstrating that algorithms with identical asymptotic complexity can exhibit substantially different practical performance depending on input characteristics.
item.dc:creator: Swastik Bhandari

item.title: On the Hardness Hierarchy for the $O(n \sqrt{\log n})$ Complexity in the Word RAM
item.description: arXiv:2503.21049v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the relative hardness of fundamental problems with state-of-the-art word RAM algorithms that take $O(n\sqrt{\log n})$ time for instances described in $\Theta(n)$ machine words ($\Theta(n\log n)$ bits). This complexity class, one of six hardness levels identified by Chan and P\u{a}tra\c{s}cu [SODA 2010], includes problems from several domains: Counting Inversions, string processing problems (BWT Construction, LZ77 Factorization, Longest Common Substring, Batched Longest Previous Factor Queries, Batched Inverse Suffix Array Queries), and computational geometry tasks (Orthogonal Range Counting, Orthogonal Segment Intersection Counting). We offer two main contributions: We establish new links between the above string problems and Dictionary Matching, a classic task solvable using the Aho-Corasick automaton. We restrict Dictionary Matching to instances with $\Theta(n)$ binary patterns of length $m = \Theta(\log n)$ each, and we prove that, unless these instances can be solved in $o(n\sqrt{\log n})$ time, the aforementioned string problems cannot be solved faster either. Via further reductions, we extend this hardness to Counting Inversions (a fundamental component in geometric algorithms) and thus to Orthogonal Range Counting and Orthogonal Segment Intersection Counting. This hinges on String Nesting, a new problem which is equivalent to Dictionary Matching and can be reduced to Counting Inversions in three steps. Together, our results unveil a single problem, with two equivalent formulations, that underlies the hardness of nearly all major problems currently occupying the $O(n\sqrt{\log n})$ level of hardness. These results drastically funnel further efforts to improve the complexity of near-linear problems. As an auxiliary outcome of our framework, we also prove that several central string problems can be efficiently reduced to their versions over the binary alphabet.
item.dc:creator: Dominik Kempa, Tomasz Kociumaka

item.title: Bandwidth vs BFS Width in Matrix Reordering, Graph Reconstruction, and Graph Drawing
item.description: arXiv:2505.10789v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We provide the first approximation quality guarantees for the Cuthull-McKee heuristic for reordering symmetric matrices to have low bandwidth, and we provide an algorithm for reconstructing bounded-bandwidth graphs from distance oracles with near-linear query complexity. To prove these results we introduce a new width parameter, BFS width, and we prove polylogarithmic upper and lower bounds on the BFS width of graphs of bounded bandwidth. Unlike other width parameters, such as bandwidth, pathwidth, and treewidth, BFS width can easily be computed in polynomial time. Bounded BFS width implies bounded bandwidth, pathwidth, and treewidth, which in turn imply fixed-parameter tractable algorithms for many problems that are NP-hard for general graphs. In addition to their applications to matrix ordering, we also provide applications of BFS width to graph reconstruction, to reconstruct graphs from distance queries, and graph drawing, to construct arc diagrams of small height.
item.dc:creator: David Eppstein, Michael T. Goodrich, Songyu Liu

item.title: A characterization of one-sided error testable graph properties in bounded degeneracy graphs
item.description: arXiv:2604.04466v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider graph property testing in $p$-degenerate graphs under the random neighbor oracle model (Czumaj and Sohler, FOCS 2019). In this framework, a tester explores a graph by sampling uniform neighbors of vertices, and a property is testable with one-sided error if its query complexity is independent of the graph size. It is known that one-sided error testable properties for minor-closed families are exactly those that can be defined by forbidden subgraphs of bounded size. However, the much broader class of $p$-degenerate graphs allows for high-degree ``hubs" that can structurally hide forbidden subgraphs from local exploration. In this work, we provide a complete structural characterization of all properties testable with one-sided error in $p$-degenerate graphs. We show that testability is determined by how copies of the forbidden graphs can share their high-degree vertices: $\mathcal{F}$-freeness is testable if and only if, for every member $H$, every set of roles of $H$ that may be played by high-degree vertices, and every pattern of dependencies between these roles, some member of $\mathcal F$ can be assembled from pieces of copies of $H$ glued according to this pattern. Our results define the exact structural boundary for testability under these constraints, accounting for both the connectivity of individual forbidden subgraphs and the collective behavior of the properties they define.
item.dc:creator: Oded Lachish, Amit Levi, Ilan Newman, Felix Reidl

item.title: Identification to Subclasses of Chordal Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2604.24325v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An identification of two vertices \(u\) and \(v\) in a graph replaces them with a new vertex that is made adjacent to every vertex of \(N(u)\cup N(v)\setminus \{u,v\}\). We study the \(\mathcal{H}\)-Identification problem, which is to decide whether a given graph \(G\) can be transformed (``identified'') to a graph in \(\mathcal{H}\) by applying at most \(k\) vertex identifications. We determine the classical and parameterized complexity of this problem for various subclasses \(\mathcal{H}\) of chordal graphs, obtaining an almost complete picture for two parameters: \(k\) and \(n-k\). We also consider the Identification problem, which is to test, for two given graphs \(G\) and \(H\), whether \(G\) can be identified to \(H\). We determine the parameterized complexity of this problem when \(H\) is a graph from one of our testbed classes, taking the number of simplicial vertices of \(H\) as the parameter.
item.dc:creator: Petr A. Golovach, Laure Morelle, Dani\"el Paulusma

item.title: Cell-Probe Lower Bounds and Complexity-Preserving Reductions for Suffix Array Queries
item.description: arXiv:2608.19172v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For a text $T$ of length $n$ over an alphabet of size $\sigma$, its suffix array lists the starting positions of the suffixes of $T$ in lexicographic order, and its inverse suffix array gives the lexicographic rank of the suffix starting at each position. Since the introduction of the FM-index and the compressed suffix array in 2000, both queries have been supported in $O((\log_\sigma n)^\epsilon)$ time using $O(n\log\sigma)$ bits, for any constant $\epsilon>0$. Yet no nontrivial time-space lower bound for suffix-array queries in compact space was known. We give the first such lower bound: in the cell-probe model with $\Theta(\log n)$-bit words, every deterministic $S$-bit data structure with $S\ge n$ answering suffix-array queries on binary strings of length at most $n$ has worst-case query time $\Omega(\log\log n/\log((S/n)\log\log n))$. Hence, structures with $O(n(\log\log n)^{O(1)})$ bits need $\Omega(\log\log n/\log\log\log n)$ query time, while constant query time requires $\Omega(n\log^\epsilon n)$ bits for some constant $\epsilon>0$, matching known upper bounds. In particular, no such $O(n)$-bit structure supports constant-time queries, answering the 25-year-old question of Grossi and Vitter. We also give exact complexity-preserving equivalences between suffix-array access and simpler prefix queries on short strings. For every $2\leq\sigma\leq n$, suffix-array queries are equivalent to prefix-select queries, and inverse-suffix-array queries are equivalent to prefix-special-rank queries. The reductions in both directions preserve all four standard measures up to constant factors: space, query time, preprocessing time, and preprocessing space. Unlike previous reductions, they incur no additive $O(\log\log n)$ query-time term. Thus, the corresponding prefix-query problems capture suffix-array and inverse-suffix-array access without asymptotic loss in any of the four measures.
item.dc:creator: Dominik Kempa, Tomasz Kociumaka

item.title: Frequency Moments Beyond Equality: Streaming Cosine Density Moments
item.description: arXiv:2609.06925v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For a stream of nonzero vectors $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb{R}^d$, let $u_i=x_i/\|x_i\|_2$. We define the cosine density of the $i$-th stream element by $D_i:=\sum_{j\in[n]}\langle u_i,u_j\rangle$ and study the density moments $M_p:=\sum_{i\in[n]}D_i^p$ in both the signed- and nonnegative-cosine regimes. These quantities are similarity-aware analogues of classical frequency moments: replacing cosine similarity by equality (that is, $D_i = \sum_{j\in[n]} \mathbf{1}\{u_j = u_i\}$) gives $M_p=F_{p+1}$ and, in particular, $M_{-1}=F_0$, the number of distinct elements. We give one-pass streaming algorithms and lower bounds whose dependence on $d$ is tight up to logarithmic factors for $p=-1$, $p=1$, and even $p \ge 2$ (the latter under signed cosine), and whose exponents differ by less than $1/2$ for odd $p \ge 3$ under nonnegative cosine. Our results thus extend several fundamental statistics from the classical data stream literature to cosine similarity, a widely used measure for comparing vector embeddings in modern AI systems. The main challenge in proving a space lower bound for nonnegative cosine is to eliminate unwanted contributions without relying on pairs of opposite vectors. We address this through a construction that we call \emph{equal-sum moment isolation}: two insertion-only prefixes have the same cardinality and vector sum, and a finite-difference comparison cancels the baseline shared by all their vectors while isolating the desired higher-order signal. This proof framework may be useful for other insertion-only streaming lower bounds, where direct cancellation is not possible.
item.dc:creator: Qin Zhang

item.title: Spatial Mixing and Deterministic Approximate Counting of Multi-spin Systems beyond Bounded Degree Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2609.12352v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a framework for deterministic approximate counting of multi-spin systems beyond bounded-degree graphs. The algorithm recursively constructs rational polytopes containing the true marginal vectors and uses linear-fractional programming to obtain certified bounds on marginal ratios. For positive interactions on graphs of polynomial connective constant $D$, we establish strong spatial mixing whenever $Dc<1$, where $c$ bounds the Birkhoff contraction coefficients of the interactions. Under the same condition, we also give a deterministic fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (\textbf{FPTAS}) for the partition function. We further extend the framework to proper colorings of sparse Erd\H{o}s-R\'{e}nyi random graphs using recursion on permissive blocks. For every fixed $\eta\in(0,1)$, sufficiently large fixed $d$, and fixed integer $q\ge(2+\eta)d$, we obtain an \textbf{FPTAS} for counting proper $q$-colorings of $G\sim\mathcal G(n,d/n)$ with high probability over $G$. This improves the leading constant $3$ in the earlier counting guarantee of Yin and Zhang (APPROX/RANDOM, 2016) to $2$, and asymptotically matches the spatial mixing regime established by Yin (ICALP, 2014).
item.dc:creator: Zhidan Li, Kuan Yang

item.title: Faster Minimum k-Cut II: Improved Randomized and Deterministic Algorithms for Weighted Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2609.27797v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Minimum $k$-Cut problem asks for a minimum-weight set of edges whose removal leaves an undirected weighted graph with at least $k$ connected components. We consider only $k\ge3$. The fastest previous algorithm for weighted graphs ran in $n^{k-2}(m+n)(\log n)^{O(k^2)}$ randomized time~\cite{LV26}; on dense graphs this is $\widetilde O_k(n^k)$, and for $k=3$ it gives an $\widetilde O(nm)$-time algorithm. We improve the dense-graph exponent from $k$ to $k-1$ and obtain the same exponent deterministically. After aggregating parallel edges in $O(m)$ time, our randomized algorithm runs with high probability in \begin{equation*} k^{O(k^2)}n^{k-1}\log^2n \end{equation*} time, while our deterministic algorithm runs in \begin{equation*} k^{O(k^2)}n^{k-1}\log^{O(1)}n \end{equation*} time. In particular, weighted Minimum $3$-Cut can be solved in $O(n^2\log^2 n)$ randomized time and in $\widetilde O(n^2)$ deterministic time. The algorithms have two main components. First, we give a faster algorithm for weighted Minimum $3$-Cut. After handling optima with a very small side and optima with two light sides, the remaining optimum has a unique structured side. Tree packing reduces its completion to a batched collection of $2$-respecting cut problems. Second, we reduce Minimum $k$-Cut to Minimum $3$-Cut by enumerating a bounded family of light-cut candidates and recursively completing either side of each candidate. If the enumeration produces too many cuts, then we can instead produce an optimum $k$-cut directly. We derandomize the $3$-cut algorithm using a deterministic near-minimum-cut skeleton, and derandomize the reduction using a specialized $4$-cut algorithm using the skeleton, the constructive light-cut bounds, and the deterministic spectral sparsifier of \cite{BSS12}.
item.dc:creator: Trevor Vaughn

item.title: Deterministic Linear-Time Modular Subset Sum
item.description: arXiv:2609.30992v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a deterministic $O(m)$-time algorithm for exact modular subset sum over every modulus $m$. The input gives distinct residues and their multiplicities. The algorithm reports all reachable residues and answers one target query. It returns a witness when the target is reachable. The algorithm uses $O(m)$ auxiliary words on an arithmetic word-RAM. This improves Pot\k{e}pa's deterministic $O(m\log m\,\alpha(m))$-time bound under the same input convention. The running time matches the cost of returning a length-$m$ Boolean array. We represent reachable residues as runs along cycles of repeated addition. Newly reached residues pay for scans of partial runs. Packed cycle flags make rebuilding take linear total time at the original modulus. A theorem on subset sums of distinct units limits the number of adaptive boundary batches to $O(m^{3/4})$. Radix sorting their $O(m)$ total keys also takes $O(m)$ time.
item.dc:creator: Phuoc Dinh Le, Kha Le

item.title: A Quantum Scaling Algorithm for Maximum-Weight Perfect Matching in General Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2609.39457v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum speed-ups have been obtained for many fundamental graph problems, including most variants of matching. A notable exception, however, is the maximum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) problem in general graphs with integer edge weights, which is arguably the most challenging variant of matching. We present a quantum algorithm for MWPM in general graphs that runs in $\widetilde{O}(n m^{2/3}\log W)$ time, where $W$ is an upper bound on the magnitude of the edge weights. This is an improvement over the best known classical combinatorial bound of $\widetilde{O}(m\sqrt n \log W)$ in the dense regime, where $m\ge n^{3/2}$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first quantum algorithm to obtain an asymptotic improvement over the best classical combinatorial algorithm for the MWPM problem in general graphs. The running time of our method accounts for QRAM initialization and access overheads up to polylogarithmic factors, as well as all classical updates to the data structures. At a high level, our algorithm is based on a classical framework due to Duan, Pettie, and Su, but our algorithm requires replacing certain classical tasks with quantum methods, alternative analysis of classical procedures, and the use of alternative data structures that can be implemented effectively in the QRAM model.
item.dc:creator: Kourosh Mirsohi, Sandy Irani, Michael T. Goodrich

item.title: Component-Weighted Centroid Search for Exact Incremental BPE
item.description: arXiv:2609.40016v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Exact incremental tokenizers keep the tokenization of a growing text up to date, so a long prompt or agent trace is not retokenized each time it grows. Jiang and Gong's algorithm does this for byte-pair encoding (BPE) in $O(\log^2 t)$ worst-case time per byte, where $t$ is the length of the longest token. Its search passes through $O(\log t)$ nested subproblems and runs a binary search over the possible branches at each one. We weight each branch by the size of the subproblem it leads to. Each step then costs about one probe for every halving of the remaining candidates, and a whole update costs $O(\log t)$, as much as one binary search over all candidates. Output and asymptotic memory are unchanged. We also construct valid BPE vocabularies on which the original search provably needs $\Theta(\log^2 t)$ probes and ours $\Theta(\log t)$, and a Rust implementation reproduces both counts exactly. On six real vocabularies the two searches run at about the same speed on ordinary text, while on long runs of spaces or hyphens the weighted search is up to 2.5$\times$ faster.
item.dc:creator: Harshit Verma, Rex Ying

item.title: Achieving Optimal Redundancy for Small Dynamic Rank/Select Dictionaries
item.description: arXiv:2610.01853v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we study the number of bits required to construct a dynamic dictionary with optimal time for $\texttt{rank}/\texttt{select}$ operations. Using the standard (multiplication) Word-RAM model with $w$-bit words, we construct a data-structure for a dynamic $\texttt{rank}/\texttt{select}$ dictionary for a set $S\subseteq\{0,1,\cdots,u-1\}$ of $n$ elements that, given a parameter $1\leq k\leq \log^*w$, uses $$\operatorname{lg}\binom{u}{n}+\mathcal{O}(n\log^{(k)}w)\text{ bits}$$ taking optimal $\mathcal{O}(k+\log_w n)$ time (worst-case) for all operations. We show optimality for $n=w^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$ and $\log u=\Theta(w)$ by extending the lower bound of Li, Liang, Yu, and Zhou [FOCS 2023] to super-polynomial universes: any dynamic dictionary for $n\leq \sqrt{u}$ elements that uses $\operatorname{lg}\binom{u}{n}+\mathcal{O}(n\log^{(k)}n)$ bits requires $\Omega(k)$ time for operations. Lastly, we extend the data-structure to a dynamic fully indexable dictionary (that also supports $\texttt{rank}/\texttt{select}$ on the complement of $S$).
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Marques Domingues

item.title: Extending Tardos's Theorem to Separable Convex Quadratic Programming
item.description: arXiv:2610.07465v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For an integer equality matrix $A\in\mathbb{Z}^{r\times m}$ of binary encoding length $\langle A\rangle$, Tardos's theorem solves linear programs using $\operatorname{poly}(r,m,\langle A\rangle)$ rational arithmetic operations and comparisons, independently of the right-hand side and objective coefficients. We extend this guarantee to continuous separable convex quadratic programming over $Ax=b$, $x\ge0$: the operation count is independent of the right-hand side, linear costs, and all nonnegative quadratic weights. The algorithm returns an exact optimal primal-dual pair or a certificate of infeasibility or unboundedness. All intermediate rational numbers have encoding lengths polynomial in the total input length. As an application, we obtain a strongly polynomial algorithm for continuous multicommodity flow with shared capacities and quadratic costs of aggregate arc flow, independently of demands, capacities, and cost coefficients. Objective compression and continuous-integer proximity yield a local solver returning a point close to an optimum. We relax nonnegativity on coordinates with zero optimal dual slack, minimize the largest remaining coordinate, and optimize over the relaxed coordinates. A descent LP over the recession cone provides a complementary bound. Circuit decomposition combines these bounds into a scale ensuring that each local call reveals a new coordinate. At most $m$ calls, followed by two LPs, recover an exact optimum and its dual certificate.
item.dc:creator: Bin Cui (Peking University), Hanqing Li (Peking University), Xupeng Miao (Peking University)

item.title: Lower Bounds for Parallel Diffusion Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2610.09166v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Standard diffusion samplers generate samples through sequential evaluations of a learned score function, with each query depending on previous answers. Parallel samplers seek to accelerate this process by making multiple score queries simultaneously. We ask how many adaptive rounds are necessary when each round allows polynomially many queries. We establish the first polynomial lower bounds on the round complexity of diffusion sampling with approximate scores satisfying a mean-square accuracy guarantee. Specifically, we prove (1) a $\widetilde{\Omega}(d^{1/3})$-round lower bound for sampling smooth, near-isotropic Gaussian mixtures in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and (2) a tight $\Omega(d)$-round lower bound for uniform sampling from anisotropic axis-aligned boxes contained in the unit ball. Both bounds hold for arbitrary randomized algorithms making polynomially many queries per round at arbitrary locations and noise levels, with inverse-polynomial score error and constant total variation accuracy. Our near-isotropic construction follows the blockwise approach of earlier lower bounds for parallel matroid search and discrete sampling \cite{KUW85,AGR24}. We use independent coordinate blocks containing random codebooks with well-separated rates and construct approximate score oracles whose responses in each block depend on consistency tests in earlier blocks. Together, the rate separation and these tests ensure that each round reveals information about at most one additional block with high probability.
item.dc:creator: Yiwen Kou, Yimeng Wang

item.title: Subset Sum via Partial Match
item.description: arXiv:2610.10446v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that the subset sum problem can be solved in randomized time $O(2^{0.49999\overline{7}n})$, breaking the $2^{n/2}$ meet-in-the-middle barrier. Our approach builds on the representation technique framework of Randolph and W\k{e}grzycki (STOC 2026). We choose a representation for which testing the compatibility of pairs of partial solution vectors is exactly the partial match problem. To beat exponent $1/2$ for subset sum, it then suffices to give a nontrivial partial match algorithm in a certain parameter regime. We achieve this by designing a depth-2 linear circuit for the partial match matrix, which yields an efficient algorithm via the framework of Alman and Li (FOCS 2025).
item.dc:creator: Baitian Li, Lixi Ye

item.title: Fast Almost-Uniform Sampling of Random $k$-SAT Solutions
item.description: arXiv:2610.10474v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study approximately uniform sampling of satisfying assignments from random $k$-SAT formulas. Fix a constant $B>0$. For every $k\ge 2^{20}$ and density $0<\alpha\le 2^k/k^{16}$, we prove that, with high probability over a random formula on $n$ variables, every accuracy $n^{-B}\le\varepsilon\le 1/2$ admits a sampler whose output distribution is within total variation distance $\varepsilon$ of the uniform distribution on satisfying assignments with expected running time $$\widetilde O_B\left(\mathrm{poly}(k,\alpha+1)n^{2+\eta}\right),\quad 0<\eta\le 2^{16-k}.$$ In particular, the exponent of $n$ is $2+O(2^{-k})$ while the dependence on the width and density is polynomial with a universal degree. This improves the parameter-dependent polynomial exponent of the sampling algorithm of Chen, Lonkar, Wang, Yang, and Yin (STOC 2025) in the density regime $2^k/\mathrm{poly}(k)$. Our algorithm separates a high-degree core from the remaining variables. Every residual formula on the good variables is a deletion subformula of a common bounded-dependency formula. Adapting the rejection--repair framework of Liu, Wang, Yin, Zhang and Zhou (arXiv 2026), we construct an executable sampler for all such residual formulas using ordinary connected violation sets replacing weighted 2-tree witnesses and use it to simulate approximate block heat-bath updates on the core. To analyze the resulting core chain, we integrate out the good variables, represent the core marginal by an absolutely convergent polymer expansion and combine a component-swap variance comparison with an adaptive exploration bound. Absorbing single-component interactions into the local weights leaves interactions of cluster size at least two; retaining their additional decay gives a spectral gap of at least $1/(2s n^{2^{12-k}})$ where $s$ counts core components. Together with the residual sampler, this yields the stated running time.
item.dc:creator: Kun He, Zhidan Li, Kuan Yang

item.title: Taxonomic Classification with Tag Arrays
item.description: arXiv:2610.10500v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Taxonomic classifiers based on exact matches differ in which matches they use and in how each match splits its credit among the taxa containing it: Kraken~2 gives a $k$-mer's credit to the lowest common ancestor of those taxa, SPUMONI~2 labels each position of the read, Tagger gives each maximal exact match (MEM) one label, and Cliffy splits a match's credit evenly over a roughly logarithmic sample of the taxa. We compare these schemes on the same long MEMs, mainly on short 16S rRNA reads classified to genera with SILVA, where credit proportional to the number of occurrences of the MEM in each taxon is the most accurate, by 1.0 to 6.8 percentage points. We compute long MEMs with Boyer--Moore--Li on a run-length compressed suffix array, and count their occurrences in each taxon with a complete, run-length compressed tag array, in time proportional to the number of tag runs in the MEM's BWT interval, without locating any occurrence. We bound the number of tag runs in terms of the BWT runs and of how often suffixes with long common prefixes have different tags, and show that tags constant on $d$ blocks of the text have a macro scheme with at most $r + 2d$ phrases. On SILVA our index takes 1.44\,GB and classifies a read in 66\,$\mu$s with one thread at 93.8\% accuracy; on the same reads and server, it is 14 times smaller than Cliffy's undigested index, and 4.4 times faster and 8 percentage points more accurate than Cliffy's LCA query on it. Over minimizer digests it takes 0.49\,GB and reaches 92.5\%; on the server, 92.1\% against 84.2\% for Cliffy's LCA query on its digested index. On nanopore reads from whole genomes, where almost every long MEM occurs in one species, we instead use each read's longest MEMs, found in one pass of a variant of Boyer--Moore--Li with a $k$-mer filter, which assigns 99.6\% of the reads to their species with no length threshold.
item.dc:creator: Travis Gagie, Gonzalo Navarro

item.title: Undirected Multiple-Unicast Network Coding and Faster External-Memory Integer Sorting
item.description: arXiv:2610.20079v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In undirected multiple-unicast networks, where independent messages are sent between specified source--destination pairs, network coding allows intermediate nodes to combine messages, whereas fractional routing splits and forwards individual messages along paths without mixing them. Proposed in 2004 by Li and Li and independently by Harvey, Kleinberg, and Lehman, the multiple-unicast conjecture---a central conjecture in network coding with deep connections to computational complexity---asserts that network coding and fractional routing have the same achievable rate region. We construct a counterexample refuting this conjecture and use it to reduce block transfers in external-memory data rearrangement, thereby accelerating external-memory integer sorting and answering in the affirmative the longstanding question of Aggarwal and Vitter (1988) on whether integer operations can beat the comparison-sorting input/output (I/O) bound. Specifically, we give a deterministic sorting algorithm: for $N$ integers of $\Theta(\log N)$ bits, a memory holding $M$ integers, and block transfers of $B$ integers, where $2B\le M\le N$, the number of block transfers is \[ O\!\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+ \frac{\log N}{(\log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(\log M)^\varepsilon} \right]\right), \] where $\varepsilon=1.5\times10^{-5}$ is an absolute constant. This bound asymptotically improves on the classical $\Theta\!\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+ \frac{\log(N/M)}{\log(M/B)}\right]\right)$ comparison-sorting bound in certain parameter regimes. Under the external-memory model specified in this paper, we have formally verified the algorithm's correctness and I/O complexity bound in Lean~4.
item.dc:creator: Baochun Li, Zongpeng Li, Sirui Liu

item.title: Tight weighted paging with delay via mirror descent
item.description: arXiv:2610.24655v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give an O(log k)-competitive randomized algorithm for weighted paging with delay. This improves upon the O(log k log n)-competitive algorithm of Gupta, Kumar, and Panigrahi (STOC 2020, SICOMP 2022) by removing the dependence on the number n of pages. Without delay, the optimal competitive ratio of randomized algorithms is Theta(log k), and since the lower bound carries over, our bound is tight. Our algorithm is fractional and combines mirror descent, used by Bubeck et al. (STOC 2018) for weighted paging without delay, with preemptive service, introduced by Azar et al. (STOC 2017) for online service with delay: when a request is served, an increase in the mirror descent potential is offset by preemptive service to other pending requests, with a budget derived from the mirror descent path. To obtain a randomized algorithm, we use the online rounding of Bansal, Buchbinder, and Naor (FOCS 2007) from classical paging.
item.dc:creator: Julian Born, Yann Disser, Linda Thelen

item.title: Improved Approximation for Unsplittable Capacitated Vehicle Routing Using Quota Trees
item.description: arXiv:2610.28501v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In the Unsplittable Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (UCVRP), we are given a set $V$ of $n$ clients with normalized demands $d_v \in (0,1]$, a depot $r$, a unit vehicle capacity, and symmetric metric travel costs $c$ on $V \cup \{r\}$. We seek a collection of routes of minimum total cost that start and end at $r$, serve each client's entire demand on a single route, and respect the unit capacity constraint $\sum_{v \in V(R)} d_v \le 1$ on every route $R$, where $V(R)$ denotes the clients served by $R$. UCVRP generalizes the metric traveling salesman problem (TSP) and is therefore NP-hard. Capacity constraints add a packing difficulty: when all clients are colocated away from the depot, minimizing the route cost is equivalent to minimizing the number of bins in bin packing. Consequently, UCVRP admits no polynomial-time approximation ratio below $3/2$ unless $\textbf{P=NP}$ (Grandoni, Mathieu, and Zhou, 2023). The classical $3.5$-approximation has been improved; Zhao and Xiao recently obtained a $(2+\ln 2+\varepsilon)$-approximation. In this paper, we give a deterministic polynomial algorithm with approximation ratio $5/2$ for general capacity and arbitrary positive demands. Our algorithm uses local search to select routes through one client with large demand and clients with small demands. It constructs candidate routes using endpoint quota trees after rounding demands and creating vertex copies. We replace selected routes using sets of two to four clients and a squared-weight local search, keeping their client sets disjoint. The remaining clients are served by partitioning a tour constructed using weighted graphic matroid parity. We also give a deterministic polynomial $5/2$-approximation algorithm for the undirected capacitated arc routing problem (CARP) with arbitrary positive edge demands.
item.dc:creator: Zhenyu Wang

item.title: Optimal Labeling Schemes for $\Gamma$-Free Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2610.29184v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study labeling schemes for $p \times q$ $\Gamma$-free binary matrices, which do not contain a submatrix of the form $\Gamma = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. We give a labeling scheme that uses $O(\log^2 N)$-bit labels for rows and columns, where $N=p+q$, such that any matrix entry can be determined from the corresponding two labels in constant time in the word RAM model. The worst-case label size matches the counting lower bound up to constant factors. We also show that the entrywise least $\Gamma$-free supermatrix of an arbitrary $p\times q$ binary matrix, together with its labels, can be constructed in $O(pq)$ time. Our construction represents a $\Gamma$-free matrix by a sequence of rooted forests, where each column corresponds to a node and the $1$-entries of each row form a root path in its corresponding forest. For $n$-vertex strongly chordal and chordal bipartite graphs, our result gives asymptotically optimal $O(\log^2 n)$-bit adjacency labeling schemes with constant-time queries. These results answer both representation questions posed by Spinrad in 1995.
item.dc:creator: Sankardeep Chakraborty, Seungbum Jo

item.title: A Tight Space Lower Bound for Pivot-Based Distance Oracles
item.description: arXiv:2610.29624v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An approximate distance oracle (ADO) is a compact data structure that answers distance queries within a multiplicative \emph{stretch} $k$. The classical oracle of Thorup and Zwick~[STOC'01, JACM'05] has stretch $k=2\ell-1$ and uses $O(\ell n^{1+1/\ell})$ space, for every integer $\ell\ge1$. This trade-off is optimal for dense graphs under the Erd\H{o}s girth conjecture. However, for sparse graphs ($m=O(n)$), their lower bound yields nothing beyond $\Omega(m)$ space. The main result of this paper is a nearly tight lower bound for pivot-based $1$-hop ADOs in sparse graphs. A pivot-based $1$-hop ADO gives every vertex $\tilde{O}(1)$ pivots and returns as an estimate the length of a walk of the form $u\to p_u \to p_v \to v$, where $p_u$ is a pivot of $u$, $p_v$ is a pivot of $v$, and $p_u\to p_v$ is a stored distance. We observe that all the state-of-the-art ADOs with $\tilde{O}(1)$ query time are in fact pivot-based $1$-hop ADOs. We prove that every \emph{pivot-based} $1$-hop ADO with \emph{real} stretch $k$ requires $\widetilde\Omega(m^{1+2/(k+1)})$ space, under the Erd\H{o}s girth conjecture for graphs with constant degree. This matches the best known ADOs with $\tilde{O}(1)$ query time, at every known stretch, up to polylogarithmic factors. We also extend our lower bound to pivot-based ADOs with any constant number $\beta$ of hops, showing that they require $\widetilde\Omega(m^{1+2/(\beta(k+1))})$ space. In addition, we obtain a tight lower bound for two-hop hopsets and improved lower bounds for general $\beta$-hop hopsets.
item.dc:creator: Avi Kadria, Liam Roditty

item.title: Constant-Factor Approximation for Non-Splitting Coflow Scheduling in Heterogeneous Parallel Networks via Iterative Relaxation
item.description: arXiv:2610.39564v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Coflows capture the collective communication requirements of data-parallel applications, and scheduling them well is essential to the performance of modern data centers. We study non-splitting coflow scheduling in a heterogeneous parallel network whose $m$ network cores may be Electronic Packet Switches (EPS), not-all-stop Optical Circuit Switches (OCS), or all-stop OCS, where every flow must be transmitted entirely through a single core. Previous approximation algorithms for this setting have guarantees that grow linearly with the number of cores $m$ or with the maximum flow degree $\tau$ of a port, and therefore become weak as data centers deploy more cores. The source of this dependence is the rounding step: rounding each flow to the core holding its largest fractional value can inflate the load of a port by a factor of $m$. We replace this step with an iterative relaxation rounding scheme that handles the input-port and output-port capacity constraints simultaneously. For minimizing the makespan, this yields approximation ratios of $\min\{\tau, 3\}$, $2\min\{\tau, 3\}$, and $4\min\{\tau, 3\}$ for pure EPS, pure not-all-stop OCS, and pure all-stop OCS networks, respectively. For minimizing the total weighted coflow completion time, we obtain approximation ratios of $8\min\{\tau, 4\}$, $16\min\{\tau, 4\}$, and $32\min\{\tau, 4\}$ for the same three architectures. In a hybrid network, the guarantee is governed by the weakest architecture present, so the overall ratios are at most $4\min\{\tau,3\}\le 12$ and $32\min\{\tau,4\}\le 128$, respectively. Unlike all previous guarantees for non-splitting coflow scheduling in heterogeneous parallel networks, these bounds are absolute constants that do not grow with the number of cores $m$ or with the flow degree $\tau$. We also show that the integrality gap of the underlying linear program is at least $2$.
item.dc:creator: Chi-Yeh Chen

item.title: Leveraging Recourse and Size Bounds for OnlineKnapsack with Removable Items
item.description: arXiv:2610.40290v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In the online unweighted knapsack problem, items arrive sequentially and must be accepted or rejected immediately for a bounded-capacity knapsack, aiming to maximize the total size of accepted items. When decisions are irrevocable, no algorithm achieves a non-trivial competitive ratio. An essential relaxation that circumvents this impossibility is to allow previously accepted items to be removed from the knapsack (a.k.a. removal). In this work, we investigate possible further improvements on the competitive ratio with removal by bringing together two other previously proposed model extensions: knowledge of an upper bound on the item sizes (a.k.a. bound awareness) and ability to reinsert previously rejected items(a.k.a.recourse). Our contributions are twofold. First, we establish close upper and lower bounds on the competitive ratio under bound awareness, removal and recourse. We show that significant improvements on the best known competitive ratio are possible when the upper bound on the item sizes is not too restrictive and only few uses of recourse are available. Second, we introduce the notion of adaptive online algorithms which do not require to know any upper bound on the item sizes but still achieve performance guarantees comparable to the ones obtained under the bound awareness model.
item.dc:creator: Dimitris Fotakis, Laurent Gourv\`es, Aris Pagourtzis, Panagiotis Patsilinakos

item.title: Multiple Swap Local Search Approximations for Uniform-Cost Capacitated Facility Location with Extensions to Outliers
item.description: arXiv:2610.41187v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study \textsc{Capacitated Facility Location}, a fundamental clustering problem, in the setting of uniform opening costs and non-uniform capacities. We give a polynomial-time $(3+\epsilon)$-approximation for this problem. Our algorithm is a multiple-swap generalization of the local search algorithm by Dabas, Garg, and Gupta (2024), who obtained a $3.732$-approximation. The main technical contribution is the analysis of this natural multiple-swap local-search method: variants of this approach have been analyzed previously, but allowing larger swaps requires new grouping and counting arguments. We also show that a multiple-swap local search algorithm provides a $(3+\epsilon)$-approximation for \textsc{Capacitated Facility Location with Outliers}, again in the same setting of uniform opening costs and non-uniform capacities. This is an improvement over the $6.372$-approximation, again by Dabas, Garg, and Gupta. Finally, we show that the factor $3$ is tight for our local-search framework, and that the same multiple-swap idea does not improve the known locality gap for the non-uniform opening-cost setting.
item.dc:creator: Zachary Friggstad, Pengfei Wu

item.title: Precomputed Dominant Resource Fairness
item.description: arXiv:2507.08846v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dominant Resource Fairness (DRF) is a resource allocation scheme, addressing the problem of fair allocation of multiple resource types among users with heterogeneous demands for different types of resources. Based on Max-min Fairness, which is a well-established algorithm in the literature for allocating resources in single resource type scenarios, DRF generalises the main principle of maximising the minimum share given to any user to the multiple resource case. It has a number of desirable properties, such as Sharing Incentive, Envy-Freeness, Pareto Efficiency, and Strategy Proofness, that make it preferable over alternatives, and as such, it is widely adopted in distributed systems. In the present study, we revisit the original study and analyse the structure of the algorithm in closer view. The main contribution is an alternative algorithm, which approximates the DRF allocation in linear time, significantly improving over the original algorithm's pseudo-polynomial runtime. We name the new algorithm Precomputed Dominant Resource Fairness (PDRF), after its main working principle. We provide bounds for approximating the original algorithm, and critically evaluate the agreements of aforementioned properties, comparing DRF and PDRF over them. It turns out that there is an adversarial strategy which forces DRF to unfairly allocate more resources to users who submit inflated demands. PDRF, on the other hand, favouring smaller demands, penalises such adversarial behaviour and creates incentive for users to submit their minimal demands.
item.dc:creator: Serdar Metin

item.title: Quantizing With Randomized Hadamard Transforms: Efficient Heuristic Now Proven
item.description: arXiv:2605.06014v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Uniform random rotations (URRs) are a common preprocessing step in modern quantization approaches used for gradient compression, inference acceleration, KV-cache compression, model weight quantization, and approximate nearest-neighbor search in vector databases. In practice, URRs are often replaced by randomized Hadamard transforms (RHTs), which preserve orthogonality while admitting fast implementations. The remaining issue is the performance for worst-case inputs. With a URR, each coordinate is distributed as a shifted beta distribution, which converges to a Gaussian distribution in high dimensions. Generally, one RHT is not suitable in the worst case, as individual coordinates can be far from these distributions. We show that after composing two RHTs on any $d$-sized input vector, the marginal distribution of every fixed coordinate of the normalized rotated vector is within $O(d^{-1/2})$ of a standard Gaussian both in Kolmogorov distance and in $1$-Wasserstein distance. We then plug these bounds into the analyses of modern compression schemes, namely DRIVE and QUIC-FL, and show that two RHTs achieve performance that asymptotically matches URRs. However, while two RHTs suffice for scalar quantization, they may be insufficient for Vector Quantization (VQ), which depends on the joint distribution across fixed-size blocks of coordinates (as opposed to only marginal distribution convergence for single coordinates). We prove that a composition of three RHTs leads to decaying coordinate covariance. This ensures that any fixed, bounded, multi-dimensional VQ codebook optimized for URRs has the same expected error when using three RHTs, up to an additive term that vanishes with the dimension. Finally, because practical inputs are rarely adversarial, we propose a linear-time $O(d)$ check on the input's moments to dynamically adapt the number of RHTs used at runtime to improve performance.
item.dc:creator: Ran Ben-Basat, William Kuszmaul, Michael Mitzenmacher, Amit Portnoy, Shay Vargaftik

item.title: Temporal Conductance and Bounds on the Voter Model for Dynamic Networks
item.description: arXiv:2606.13374v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The voter model is a classical stochastic process that models how opinions might spread through a network: at each step, every node lazily adopts the opinion of a random neighbour; eventually all nodes share the same opinion (consensus). Stronger connectivity should yield faster consensus. Berenbrink, Giakkoupis, Kermarrec, and Mallmann-Trenn (ICALP 2016) make this precise via the network's conductance: if the network has $m$ edges, minimum degree $d_{\min}$, and conductance at least $\phi$, then the voter model reaches consensus in expected $O(m/(d_{\min}\phi))$ steps. Their results extend to dynamic networks with fixed vertex degrees by considering the network's conductance at each time step. We introduce temporal conductance $\Phi$, a more general connectivity measure for dynamic networks. Unlike static conductance, which collapses to $0$ whenever some snapshot is disconnected, $\Phi$ captures connectivity through edges that appear at different times. We generalise the results of Berenbrink et al. from static conductance to temporal conductance, showing that the expected consensus time of the standard voter model is at most $O(m/(d_{\min}\Phi))$. Moreover, we prove that this bound is tight up to constant factors. We expect temporal conductance to be a useful primitive for analysing other dynamics on temporal networks, and potentially time-inhomogeneous Markov chains more generally.
item.dc:creator: Tatiana Rocha Avila, Holger Dell, John Lapinskas

item.title: Coresets for Continuous $k$-Center in Hyperbolic Space
item.description: arXiv:2606.16061v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study coresets for the continuous $k$-center problem in fixed-dimensional hyperbolic space $\mathbb H^D$, where centers may lie anywhere in the space. For an input set $P$ of $n$ points, we construct an unweighted coreset of size $(k/\varepsilon)^{O(kD)}$ in $O(nkD(k/\varepsilon)^{O(kD)})$ time, independent of the enclosing radius. Every exact optimal solution for the coreset is a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for $P$. The same construction also yields a strong coreset after adjusting the accuracy parameter. Our method combines local Euclidean grids at bounded scales with radial shells at larger scales. Hyperbolic balls induce spherical caps on representative spheres, whose multiplicative enlargement can be controlled by additive hyperbolic distance errors. A recursive ball-coverage certificate then selects a radius-independent set of input witnesses. We establish lower bounds of $\Omega_D(k\varepsilon^{-D})$ for $k\ge 8D$ and sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, and $2^{\Omega(k)}$ for $D\ge2$ when $\varepsilon=\Theta(1/k)$, ruling out bounds polynomial jointly in $k$ and $1/\varepsilon$. For $k$ sufficiently separated clusters, we obtain simultaneous additive and multiplicative weak coreset guarantees, with optimal worst-case size $\Theta_D(k\varepsilon^{-(D-1)/2})$ when both errors equal $\varepsilon$. In contrast, even under the same separation condition, no radius-independent additive weak coreset bound exists in the Euclidean plane for $k=2$.
item.dc:creator: Eunku Park

item.title: Dynamic estimation of slowly varying sequences
item.description: arXiv:2606.23655v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We consider the problem of sequentially approximating a target function of each element in a slowly-varying sequence, i.e. one where the magnitude $\alpha_i$ of the difference between the elements at positions $i$ and $i-1$, measured in an appropriate norm, is small. Recent work on implicit trace estimation shows that when $\alpha_i$ is small in Frobenius norm, reusing queries to past sequence elements can reduce the overall cost. We introduce a framework that generalizes this approach to linear and nonlinear functions on normed vector spaces, obtaining sequential estimation results for matrix powers, spectral densities, Monte Carlo integration, and certain boundary value problems from partial differential equations~(PDEs). Furthermore, we develop an algorithm that locally scales the estimation budget with $\alpha_i$, obtaining sharper path-length-style variation bounds of the form $\mathcal{O}\left(\tfrac1{\epsilon^2}\sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i\right)$ on the cost of estimating a sequence of length $m$ to accuracy $\epsilon$. This improves upon the earlier implicit trace estimation dependence on $\tfrac m{\epsilon^2}\max_i\alpha_i$, which results from fixing the query budget using the worst-case step size $\alpha_i$ and is thus inefficient for stable sequences with rare bursts. Furthermore, while prior theoretical guarantees assume a known bound on the step sizes, we show in certain cases how to estimate them on the fly with (nearly) no added cost. Lastly, we complement our theoretical results with experiments demonstrating improved accuracy-cost trade-offs over prior baselines on trace estimation and Hessian tracking. In summary, our framework makes sequential approximation general-purpose and adaptive while sharpening state-of-the-art guarantees for dynamic trace estimation.
item.dc:creator: Prashant Gokhale, Mikhail Khodak, Sandeep Silwal

item.title: A Forward-Backward Weight Analysis of INW for Permutation Branching Programs
item.description: arXiv:2607.18168v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We construct an $\varepsilon$-error PRG for permutation read-once branching programs of length $n$ and width $w$ with seed length \[ O\left((\log w+\log(1/\varepsilon))\cdot \log n\right). \] This gives an exponential improvement in the dependence on $w$ compared with the constructions of De (CCC 2011) and Steinke (ECCC 2012). Compared with the work of Braverman, Rao, Raz, and Yehudayoff (FOCS 2010; SICOMP 2014), which applies more generally to regular branching programs and already achieves the optimal dependence on $w$, our result improves the dependence on the length $n$, attaining the optimal logarithmic dependence. The generator itself is the classical INW PRG of Impagliazzo, Nisan, and Wigderson (STOC 1994). We show that, for permutation branching programs, the INW generator can be instantiated with expanders whose degrees are polynomial in $w$ and $1/\varepsilon$ and, crucially, independent of $n$. To prove this, we analyze error propagation using program-dependent seminorms tailored to the branching program at hand. These seminorms build on the weight function introduced by Braverman et al. The key point is that, when measured in these adapted seminorms, the error does not accumulate throughout the recursion. Since our analysis relies only on the spectral expansion of the underlying expanders, our seed length tightly matches the recent lower bound for spectral analyses of the INW generator due to Hoza, Pyne, and Vadhan (Algorithmica 2024).
item.dc:creator: Gil Cohen, Dean Doron, Noam Goldgraber

item.title: Streaming Right Multiplication over Grammar-Compressed Matrices: A Memory-Bounded GPU Engine for Genotype and Graph Data
item.description: arXiv:2607.24971v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Grammar-compressed matrices store a matrix's non-zero structure as a RePair straight-line program (SLP), supporting matrix-vector products in time and space proportional to the compressed size. We target the regime where this is decisive on a GPU: when the uncompressed matrix exceeds device memory, so footprint (not floating-point throughput) is the binding constraint. Our SLP is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of out-degree 2, and the right product $y=Mx$ is a single bottom-up sweep (leaves to roots): a conflict-free gather. We make the grammar properly layered (every nonterminal child one level below its parent) via pass-through completion, which inserts identity nodes to carry values upward until consumed. This yields a streaming evaluation in which each level reads only the level below and writes the next, so the live set fits in two alternating read-only/write-only buffers instead of scaling with the whole grammar. On genotype matrices, where a polygenic score is exactly the right product $y=G\beta$, a CUDA implementation shows a clear space advantage: a device footprint 3.5 to 8 times smaller than a materialized cuSPARSE CSR baseline, single-vector times within a small factor of cuSPARSE, and consistently lower GPU energy. Because the sweep needs only an associative and commutative combine, the same engine evaluates any homomorphism into a commutative monoid over the grammar by swapping a small leaf/combine/emit policy; the same reachability sweep scales to a billion-edge Software Heritage graph (261 TB dense, 21 times smaller serialized than cuSPARSE's CSR). We frame this as an algorithm-engineering case study: structural metrics (depth, live-set width, completion cost) are measured, architecture-independent grammar properties, whereas time and energy are profiled on a single board.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Tosoni, Gabriele Mencagli

item.title: Exponential Quantum Advantage in Testing Fourier Dimensionality
item.description: arXiv:2609.25816v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A boolean function $f$ has Fourier dimension $k$ if its strings with nonzero Fourier coefficients span a subspace of dimension $k$. We first consider the property testing task of determining whether a function has Fourier dimension at most $k$, or is $\epsilon$-far from being so. We show that there is an $O(k/\sqrt{\epsilon})$-query quantum property tester for this problem, which we show to be almost optimal. Combined with Gopalan \etal's classical lower bound of $\Omega(2^{k/2})$, this demonstrates an exponential quantum advantage for this task. We complement this result with a $\tilde{O}(2^{k/2}/\epsilon)$ classical tester, giving a quadratic improvement over the previous best tester, and essentially settling the classical query complexity. We then introduce and study the tolerant version of this problem. That is, determining whether a function is $\alpha\epsilon$-close to having Fourier dimension at most $k$, or is $\epsilon$-far from being so. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that this tolerant version of the problem is essentially just as hard as the standard version of the problem. That is, we show this problem has a $\tilde{O}(k/\epsilon)$ quantum tester, and a $\tilde{O}(2^{k/2}/\epsilon)$ classical tester.
item.dc:creator: Kenny Chen

item.title: A Tale of Two Walks: From Kac to KMP and Back
item.description: arXiv:2609.38044v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We reveal an unexpected connection between two interacting particle systems: Kac's walk and the Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti (KMP) process. We first establish a mixing-time analogue of Aldous's conjecture for the KMP process on general graphs: the mixing time of the $t$-particle process on any connected $d$-vertex graph is at most $O(\log d)$ times the corresponding single-particle mixing time, uniformly in $t$. As an application, we improve the mixing-time bound for coordinate hit-and-run on the $n$-dimensional standard simplex from $\widetilde{O}(n^3)$ [KV26] to $O(n\log n)$, while removing the dependence on the initial distribution. We then show that the twirling channel induced by the parallel Kac's walk on the symmetric subspace can be exactly encoded by a Markov chain on partitions, which naturally lifts to a parallel KMP chain on the complete graph. We prove that $O(\log d+\log(1/\varepsilon))$ repetitions of the parallel Kac's walk suffice to approximate Haar twirling on the symmetric subspace of $(\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes t}$ to error $\varepsilon$, uniformly in all $t$. Our main technical contribution is a new structural property of KMP-type dynamics: conditional product structure, which holds for both the standard KMP processes on general graphs and the parallel KMP processes on complete graphs. Conditioned on suitable auxiliary randomness, the evolution of the labeled KMP process factorizes into independent single-particle updates. Combining this structure with an exact coupling inspired by the analysis of Kac's walk, we remove the dependence on the number of particles from the mixing bounds for both unlabeled KMP models. This bypasses the $\log(\pi_{\min}^{-1})$ dependency from spectral-gap arguments, which is often prohibitively large for many-particle systems. Using this framework, we prove mixing bounds that are sharp up to logarithmic factors for both unlabeled KMP models.

item.title: Rapid Mixing for Sampling Colorings of Random Graphs up to Tree Uniqueness Threshold
item.description: arXiv:2610.25391v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the mixing time of the single-site Glauber dynamics for sampling proper $q$-colorings on sparse Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi random graphs $\mathcal{G}(n, d/n)$. We prove that, whenever $q \ge (1 + o_d(1))d$, Glauber dynamics mixes in polynomial time with high probability over $\mathcal{G}(n, d/n)$ for all sufficiently large integers $n$. This improves the previous bound $q = (\alpha^* + o_d(1))d$ where $\alpha^* = 1.7632...$ is the unique solution of $x = \exp(1/x)$ on $[1, \infty)$ by Efthymiou, Hayes, \v{S}tefankovi\v{c}, and Vigoda (SODA, 2018) and asymptotically matches the uniqueness threshold on infinite regular trees. Our proof has three main ingredients. First we establish logarithmic bounds on the spectral and coupling independence constants of the Gibbs distribution by extending the tree analysis of Chen, Liu, Mani, and Moitra (J. ACM, 2026). Second, we extend the entropy-factorization framework for two-spin systems on random graphs, developed by Bez\'akov\'a, Galanis, Goldberg, and \v{S}tefankovi\v{c} (TALG, 2024), to proper colorings by introducing a buffer around high-degree vertices. Finally, we compare the resulting heat-bath block dynamics with the single-site Glauber dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Zhidan Li, Kuan Yang

item.title: Unconditional Lower Bounds for the Fredman--Khachiyan Algorithms for Monotone Boolean Duality Testing
item.description: arXiv:2610.34474v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove unconditional lower bounds on the number of recursive calls made by the two algorithms of Fredman and Khachiyan (1996) for monotone Boolean duality testing, as a function of the explicit input size $N$. For Algorithm A we show a lower bound of $N^{\Omega(\log N)}$ on the dual pairs $(\HH_k,\LL_k)$ obtained from the read-once family of Gurvich and Khachiyan. The proof lower-bounds the number of leaves of every binary decision tree computing the function by the modulus of its multilinear polynomial evaluated at a complex point of the unit circle. It therefore applies to every choice of branching variables and, more generally, to the class of two-child variable-restriction procedures whose terminal calls have polynomially bounded decision-tree complexity. On this family the number of calls is exactly $N^{\Theta(\log N)}$. For Algorithm B, a symmetric specialization of the polynomial padding construction of Kobayashi, Kurita, and Wasa, with full polynomial blocks, yields at least $q^{(t-1)k-t(t-1)/2}$ calls, where $k=4t^2$ and $q=\Theta(t^2)$; as a function of $N$ this is $N^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log N/\log\log N})}$ along an infinite family. In an appendix we show that applying the padding construction directly to Algorithm A gives $\Omega(2^n)$ calls on a dual pair obtained from an unsatisfiable $n$-variable formula, which is only $N^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log N/\log\log N})}$ in terms of the input size. No complexity-theoretic assumption is used. The proofs allow every branching-variable choice permitted by the respective algorithm. They concern the original recursive procedures, counting every invocation separately, without sharing calls or adding positive stopping tests.
